en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Eighty,
Cūḷahaṃsa-vagga (The Lesser Goose Chapter)
5. The Mahāsutasoma Jātaka “Why, O Rasaka,
do you perform such exceedingly cruel deeds?”
“I have led astray women and men,
deluded by the sake of meat or for the sake of wealth.
“It was not for my own sake, nor for the sake of wealth;”
“Not for my children, wife, friends, or kinsmen;
the Blessed One is my lord and protector of the earth,
yet he eats meat such as this, O Venerable Sir.”
“If you, engaged for the sake of your husband,
perform such extremely cruel deeds;
having reached the inner palace even at dawn— ”
“You shall lick it in the presence of the King.
“I will do so, Venerable Sir,
just as you say, Kāḷahatthi.”
"Having reached the inner palace early in the morning,
I will speak that to you in the presence of the king.
Then, at the end of the night,
At the rising of the sun,
Kāḷa, taking a vessel of broth,
approached the king.
Having approached the king,
he spoke these words:
"Is it true, O Great King?"
This poison was sent by you;
it kills both women and men,
yet you yourself eat its flesh.”
“In this very way, Kāḷa,
the messenger was sent by me;
while he was working for my benefit, [he was struck down].”
"Why do you revile me?
Ānanda, having eaten all the fish,
you were greedy for their flavor."
When his retinue has perished,
he dies having devoured himself;
thus does one who is heedless, addicted to the pride of taste, [perish].
If a fool does not understand when he comes [to this state],
having abandoned his children and kinsmen who have strayed from the Dhamma,
he devours only himself by turning back upon himself.
Having heard this, let your desire depart;
O King, do not eat human flesh.
Do not consume this entirely, like a water-dweller.
The lord of bipeds made the kingdom empty.
There was one named Sujāta by name,
his own legitimate son born from his body.
O Kāḷa, just as one who has traveled the distance across Jambudīpa perishes when his provisions are exhausted, even so am I.
Having eaten food of the highest flavor,
yet not having obtained human flesh,
I think I shall give up my life.
“Young man, you are handsome and born into a well-born family;
you do not deserve this, dear one.”
"Should I eat what is not fit to be eaten?
"This is one of the flavors;
why do you forbid me from it?"
I shall go there,
where I may obtain such as this; thus I shall emerge.
I will not go into your presence,
O brahmin, you who do not rejoice at the sight of me.
“Surely we shall obtain other heirs and sons, young man;
as for you, wretch, you shall perish!”
“Where the bowl is, there one does not hear [the sound].
“In just this way, O King,
lord of bipeds, listen to me:”
“They will banish you from the kingdom,
like a drunken young man.
“He who is known by the name Sujāta— ”
The disciple who has cultivated himself,
like one longing for a snap of the fingers,
neither ate nor drank.
Just as one might take a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass and measure it against the waters of the ocean,
so too are human sensual pleasures.
In the presence of the celestial deities. Just so, Kāḷa,
having eaten food of the most excellent flavor, I—
“Having failed to obtain human flesh,
I think I shall give up my life.
“Just as it is for you, Dhatarattha,” [he said].
Like swans traveling through the sky,
they have all passed away without further enjoyment.
In the same way, O King,
lord of bipeds, listen to me:
you have eaten what is not to be eaten, O King.
Therefore they cause you to be expelled.
Though I told you, "Stay!",
you go away with your face turned back.
"You are not established, yet you say,
'I am established,' O female practitioner of the holy life;
this is unbecoming of a recluse for you."
"And you think I am a heron-feathered arrow.
"I stand, O King, among those of my own dharma;
I do not change my name or lineage."
They say that one who stands in the world with a corrupt mind,
having passed away from here, is destined for a state of loss and rebirth in hell.
If you have faith, O King—
"Take up what has been heard, O Kshatriya;
having performed a sacrifice with that,
you will thus go to heaven."
“In what country is your birthplace?
For what purpose have you come here?
Tell me this matter, O brahmin.”
"What do you desire? I shall give it to you today as requested.
"O Lord of the Earth, four verses of profound meaning, comparable to the noble ocean;"
"I have come here for your very sake;
listen to these verses endowed with the ultimate meaning.
"The wise, possessed of discernment, do not weep."
Those who are learned and contemplate many things—
this indeed is the supreme island for humans,
that the wise become dispellers of sorrow.
Whether it be yourself, your kinsmen, or your children and wife;
grain, wealth, silver, or gold— why, Sutasoma,
do you not grieve for these?
“O merchant Koraavya, let us hear those words of yours.
“I do not praise myself, nor my children and wife, nor wealth, nor the kingdom.”
The ancient Dhamma of the virtuous has been practiced;
that confusion caused distress to the brahmin.
"Confusion was created by me, a brahmin."
While remaining in my own kingdom and sovereignty,
I shall return again as one who guards the truth,
having cleared away that confusion from the lineage of the brahmins.
“I do not believe this: that a man who has escaped from the jaws of death could be happy,
or that he might again fall into the hands of his enemies.”
"Koravya, the merchant did not approach me.
You have been released from the hands of the man-eater;
go to your own palace and enjoy all your desires."
“O King, having obtained a life that is sweet and dear,
how could you come into my presence as one who is dead?
“One of pure virtue would choose death.”
One of evil nature is not praised for his life,
for he does not protect that man from miserable states,
even for whose sake he might speak untruth.
Even if the wind were to carry away a mountain,
and the moon and sun were to fall to the ground,
and all rivers were to flow upstream—
But I would never speak a falsehood, O King,
even if the sky were to split asunder, the ocean were to dry up,
and the earth that sustains all beings were to be consumed.
Mount Meru, the accumulation of rock,
might rise up together with its very roots, but I, O King, would never speak a falsehood.
I grasp both the sword and the spear.
I shall even take an oath upon you, my friend:
once released by you and being free from debt,
I will return again, guarding my truth.
“The promise that was made to you by the brahmin,
who stood in the sovereignty of his own kingdom—
that promise, O brahmin, fulfill it with excellence.”
"Protecting the truth, come back again.
"The promise that was made to me by the brahmin,
while he stood in the sovereignty of his own kingdom— "
Having fulfilled that promise to the excellent brahmin,
I shall return again, guarding my truth.
And he was released from the hands of the man-eater.
Having approached that brahmin, he said this to him:
"We would hear those verses worth a hundred coins,
O Brahmā, which, when heard by us, would be for our welfare."
“O Sutasoma, meeting with the virtuous occurs only once in a while;
that association preserves one.”
Do not associate much with the unvirtuous;
dwell only with the virtuous,
and cultivate intimacy with the virtuous.
Having understood the true Dhamma,
one becomes better, not worse.
Indeed, even beautifully adorned royal chariots wear out.
Thus even the body falls into decay;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay,
for the good proclaim it to the good.
The sky is far, and the earth is far;
they say the further shore of the ocean is far;
but they say that is indeed far compared to this.
“The Dhamma of the virtuous and the non-virtuous, O King.
“These verses are worth a thousand;
these verses are not worth a hundred.”
“Take four thousand [pieces of gold],
O Brahmin, quickly.
“[I have] eighty or ninety verses,” he said.
Even a verse of sixteen lines may exist;
know for yourself, Sutasoma,
what kind of verse there might be called "The Thousandfold."
“I desire for myself the growth of wisdom through hearing,
so that the virtuous may associate with me as one who is peaceful;
just as the great ocean receives the flowing rivers, I [shall receive them].”
For I am not satiated by your well-spoken words, dear one,
just as fire is not satiated while burning grass and wood,
nor is the ocean satiated by rivers.
In this way, O best of kings, those wise ones do not grow weary even after hearing well-spoken words.
When I hear [the teachings] from Sakka’s servant, I am never satiated.
O Lord of Men, I shall recite a verse endowed with meaning;
listen to it with careful attention,
for there is no satiety for me regarding the Dhammas, my dear father.
This kingdom of yours, with its wealth and its equipment,
along with your own life-span and all objects of desire—
is it for the sake of these pleasures that you revile me?
“I am going to inform the man-eater.
“These elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers exist for the sake of self-protection.”
“Let us employ the cavalry and the archers;
let us mobilize the army and slay the enemy.
“Porisāda has done what is very difficult to do.”
Having taken hold of me, he released me;
remembering that former service of his,
O Lord of Men, how could I betray him?
Having paid homage to his father and mother,
and having instructed the citizens and the army, he,
a speaker of truth, remained devoted to truth.
He arrived where Porisāda was.
"A pact was made by me with the brahmin,
while I remained in sovereignty over my own kingdom."
Having fulfilled that promise, O Brahmin,
I have returned as one who guards the truth;
perform your sacrifice and eat me, O man-eater!
“It does not diminish what I have eaten afterwards;
this funeral pyre is still smoky.
When it is smokeless, what is cooked will be well-prepared.”
“Let us hear verses that are worth a hundred pieces of gold.
“You have acted unrighteously, O man-eater;
you have been expelled from the kingdom for the sake of your belly.”
Where do these verses that praise the Dhamma,
and where do the Dhamma and the non-Dhamma meet?
[They meet] in one who is unrighteous and cruel.
They are constantly blood-handed;
there is no truth, so how could there be Dhamma?
What will you do with your learning?”
“He who would go hunting for the sake of meat,
or he who might kill a man for the sake of wealth—
both of them, having passed away, become equal.”
"Why do you call me one who acts contrary to the Dhamma?
"Five kinds of food are not to be eaten by a wise Kshatriya."
“O King, you ate what should not be eaten;
therefore, you are unrighteous.
“You have been released from the hands of the man-eater.”
Having gone to your own palace,
you who desired pleasure have returned again into the hands of your enemies;
you are not skilled in the duty of a noble, O King.
“Those who are skilled in the duties of a kshatriya generally become denizens of hell;
therefore, having abandoned the duties of a kshatriya, I— ”
“Guarding the truth, I have returned;
offer the sacrifice and eat me, O man-eater!
“Dwelling in palaces, possessing land, cattle, and horses,”
"Desirable women and Kāsi cloth and sandalwood—
all these you obtain there because of your master;
what benefit do you see in truth?"
“Whatever flavors exist on this earth,
truth is the most excellent among those flavors;
and the recluses and brahmins who are established in truth— ”
They cross to the further shore of birth and death.
“You have been released from the hands of the man-eater;
having gone to your own home, you may enjoy all desires as you wish.”
You have returned again into the hands of your enemies;
surely, O Lord of Men, you have no fear of death,
for you are one whose mind is undaunted and who speaks the truth.
“Various kinds of wholesome deeds have been performed by me;
those vast and praised sacrifices have been offered.
The path to the world beyond has been purified.”
Established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
By me have been performed many kinds of wholesome deeds,
and sacrifices have been offered that are vast and praised.
I shall go to the next world without remorse;
perform the sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me to them.
My father and mother are waiting for me.
My sovereignty is praised for being in accordance with the Dhamma;
the path to the world beyond has been purified.
Established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
Both my father and mother were supported by me;
my sovereignty was praised for being exercised in accordance with the Dhamma;
I shall go to the next world without remorse.
Sacrifice the sacrifice; eat me, O man-eater!
I have performed services for my kinsmen and friends, and my sovereignty is praised for being exercised in accordance with the Dhamma.
The path to the world beyond has been purified;
established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
The services I have performed for my kinsmen and friends—
My sovereignty is praised for being in accordance with the Dhamma;
I shall go to the next world without remorse.
Perform your sacrifice, O Porisada, and give me away as the offering.
I have given gifts in many ways to many,
and I have satisfied recluses and brahmins;
the path to the world beyond has been purified.
Established in the Dhamma, who would fear death?
I have given gifts in many ways to many,
and I have satisfied recluses and brahmins.
“I shall go to the next world without remorse;
offer the sacrifice, give me up, O Porisāda.
“A man who gives poison to people should not be given [anything].”
Even his head would shatter into seven pieces if he were to reject such a speaker of truth,
who is like a venomous snake blazing with fierce heat.
Having heard the Dhamma,
people discern what is wholesome and what is evil,
even after hearing just a single verse.
“My mind delights in the Dhamma.
“O Great King, one meets with the virtuous but once;”
Association protects him;
one should not have much contact with the unwholesome.
One should dwell only with the wise.
One should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
by understanding the true Dharma of the noble ones,
one becomes better, not worse.
Indeed, well-adorned royal chariots decay,
and likewise the body also succumbs to old age;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not decay.
The virtuous proclaim this to the virtuous:
"The sky is far, the earth is far,
and they say the further shore of the ocean is far."
"Therefore, O King, they say that the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the unvirtuous are indeed far apart.
"These verses are meaningful and well-phrased," [he said].
"Having heard your well-spoken words,
O Lord of Men, I am joyful, glad, cheerful, and delighted;
O Noble One, I grant you four boons."
“You who perceive for yourself your own death,
as well as what is beneficial and harmful, the states of ruin, and heaven;
yet you are greedy for flavors and settled in misconduct— ”
"What boon will you grant, O one of evil nature?
I shall consider it a fault if you do not grant me the boon that I request,
and if you, having granted it, should then revoke it."
“Who that is wise, knowing this quarrel and dispute to be so evident, would go forth [into homelessness]?
It is not right for a person to give such a gift.”
Or even if, having given something, one should later regret it,
you should grant a boon, my dear, without wavering—
even at the cost of sacrificing your own life.
“The noble one’s friendship accords with the noble,
and the wise one’s accords with the wise;
one might see such a person for a hundred years in good health.”
“This is the first of the boons I choose:
‘The friendship of the noble with the noble is fitting;
the wisdom of the wise accords with the wise.’”
“May you see me healthy for a hundred years;
this I grant as the first of my boons.
“As for those kṣatriyas here who are protectors of the earth...”
"Anointed on the head and given a name— such a lord of the earth has not been granted by any other king.
This second boon I choose."
“As for those kṣatriyas here who are protectors of the earth,
consecrated on the head and given their names—
I do not give such lords of the earth.”
“This is the second of the boons I grant.
“More than a hundred kṣatriyas have been taken captive;
they are weeping with tearful faces, like talāvutas.”
“Entrust these kingdoms to him;
this third boon I choose.
“I have already accepted more than a hundred kṣatriyas,” [the king replied].
“Tearful and weeping with faces bathed in tears,
I shall restore you to your own kingdom;
this I give as the third of your boons.”
“Your kingdom is riddled with holes, for people are trembling with fear;
many men have entered into hiding places.
O King, desist from eating human flesh!”
“This is the fourth boon I choose.
“Surely that food is pleasing to my mind;
it was for the sake of this that I entered the forest.”
"How could I desist from this?
Grant me another boon as the fourth, O Lord of Men.
"One such as I, O King, does not say, 'This is dear to me'."
Having disregarded oneself, one pursues what is dear;
yet the self alone is better than the highest other,
for what is dear can be obtained later by one who has cultivated the true goal.
“Human flesh is dear to me, Sutasoma; know this well.
It is not possible for me to turn back.”
"Choose another boon, my dear. "One who,
thinking 'this is dear to me,' protects what is dear,
yet disregards his own self while indulging in those things he holds dear— "
Like an elephant that has drunk a poisoned drink,
he becomes miserable because of that very thing in the future.
But he who, having understood this, abandons all endearments here—
One practices the noble Dhamma even with difficulty; like one who,
being afflicted, has drunk medicines,
he becomes happy thereby in the future world.
“Having abandoned both my father and mother,
as well as the five pleasing strands of sensual pleasure,
I have entered the forest for this purpose.”
“What boon shall I grant you? [The king replied:
“The wise do not speak words with double meaning;
the virtuous remain true to their promise.”
“‘Varaṃsu samma’—thus you spoke to me;
‘Iccabravī tvaṃ na hi te sameti.
[This brings] the acquisition of demerit, ill-repute, and infamy.”
"Much evil, misconduct, and defilement he has brought upon himself for the sake of human flesh;
how could I give that to you as a boon?"
“A person should not give a gift that they might later regret; choose a boon,
my dear, without wavering.”
Even after giving up their lives, the virtuous still desire only the Dhamma.
The virtuous do not give up the Dhamma for the sake of their lives;
rather, the virtuous remain true to their promise.
Having granted the boon, fulfill it quickly;
by this means, O best of excellent kings, attain perfection.
Sacrifice wealth for the sake of the most precious limb.
One may sacrifice a limb while protecting one's life;
a person mindful of the Dhamma may sacrifice a limb, wealth, and even their entire life.
For when a person understands the Dhamma,
and the virtuous remove his doubt,
that indeed becomes for him an island and a refuge.
“By that, a wise person’s friendship would not decay.
“Indeed, that food is pleasing to me;
it was for its sake that I entered the forest.”
And if you entreat me for this matter,
my friend, I shall grant you this boon as well:
you shall be both my teacher and my friend.
“I have also carried out your word, my friend;
you too, my friend, carry out my word.
Let us both go and set [him] free.”
“I am both your teacher and your friend;
you have indeed heeded my word, my dear friend.
I too shall heed your word, my dear friend.”
“Let us both go and set them free.
“Afflicted by Kammāsapāda, the Talāvutas,
with tearful faces, are weeping.”
“Never betray this king;
grant me your promise of truth.
“We have been harassed by Kammāsapāda.”
With tears on our faces and weeping, we say:
"We shall never be unfaithful to this king;
we promise to honor your word of truth."
“Just as a father or likewise a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their offspring,
even so let it be for you, and for this king.”
"And may you be to us just like sons.
"Just as a father or likewise a mother is compassionate and desires the welfare of their offspring;"
"Let it not be so; let this king and we ourselves also become his sons. [He said:
"The flesh of quadrupeds and even of birds..."
Cook well, prepare it thoroughly, and finish it perfectly;
then, like Indra enjoying ambrosia, eat it yourself.
Why do you abandon this and take delight in the forest?
Those kṣatriya women, adorned and standing in the midst of the flower-pavilion,
surrounded him and delighted him like Indra among the gods.
Having abandoned conversation, why do you delight in the forest?
Why do you not enjoy the beautiful, well-furnished bed with many woolen covers, amidst all the comforts of your home?
Having slept comfortably in the middle of a fine bed,
why have you left it and now delight in the forest?
Why do you sit at the base of a pillar with your hands as a drum?
Moreover, having abandoned even a band of musicians—
though devoid of men— and much well-sung and well-played music,
why do you take delight in the forest?
Possessing well-maintained parks and abundant garlands,
the city was delightful and filled with deer-skin clad ascetics;
it was provided with horses, elephants, and chariots.
“Having abandoned [the world], why do you delight in the forest?
“As the moon in the dark fortnight wanes day by day;”
O King, the assembly of the wicked is like the dark fortnight;
just as I have come for the sake of the essence.
I committed a wicked deed as a cook, the lowest of base men,
by which I am now going to a state of misery.
Just as the moon in the bright fortnight increases day by day,
O King, you are like that bright fortnight.
There is a meeting with the virtuous. Just as I have come to you,
Sutasoma, understand this.
I shall perform wholesome karma by which I may go to a happy destination.
Just as water poured upon dry land, O Lord of Men, [does not stay].
Not lasting long and not enduring for a while—
thus is the meeting of the wicked,
transient like water on dry land.
Just as water that has fallen upon the earth remains for a long time,
O Lord of Men, best of heroes among men,
even so indeed is the meeting of the virtuous.
The meeting of the virtuous is imperishable, like water in a lake that remains for a long time;
even as long as it lasts, it remains just so.
For quickly does one depart from the company of the wicked;
therefore, the Dhamma of the virtuous is far removed from the unrighteous.
He is no king who conquers one who cannot be conquered.
He is no friend who betrays his friend;
she is no wife who does not fear her husband;
they are no sons who do not support their aged parents.
That is no assembly where the virtuous are not present;
they are not virtuous who do not speak the Dhamma.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion—
The virtuous become known only when they speak the Dhamma;
for one who does not speak,
the wise man cannot be distinguished from fools.
They know him as he speaks,
teaching the deathless state;
let him speak and illuminate the Dhamma.
One should raise up the banner of the seers;
for the seers have well-spoken words as their banner,
since the Dhamma is indeed the banner of the seers.
The Mahāsutasoma Jātaka, the fifth.
The Asīti Nipāta is finished.
Its summary verse:
Then there was Sumukha, the great and excellent swan,
and another most noble one who fed on nectar;
and Bhayana, the lord of birds, the son of Sakunāla.
Sutasoma, Varu, Uttama, and Savhaya.
